passage:
'Oh no. My sketch pens are on the dining table at home,' Mahima groaned as the art teacher handed out paper.
'Take mine,' Usha said, sliding the packet across. 'I'll use the crayons.'
'Really? You don't mind?'
'It's fine. Your peacock needs the green more than my house does.'
Mahima drew all period, humming. When the bell rang, she stuffed the pens into her bag with her own things.
Three days later, Usha tapped her shoulder at the water cooler. 'Mahima, you still have my sketch pens, na? I need them for the chart tomorrow.'
Mahima's hand flew to her mouth. 'I totally forgot! Sorry, sorry. I'll bring them first thing.'
'No problem. Your peacock was lovely, by the way.'
Next morning the packet was on Usha's desk, with a toffee on top.

qa.q: Where had Mahima left her sketch pens?
qa.a: On the dining table at home.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she handed over her pens?
qa.a: Generous and relaxed; she expected nothing back and was happy that Mahima's peacock would get the green 🙂

qa.q: How did Usha handle the pens not coming back?
qa.a: She asked politely and simply, saying she needed them for the chart, without blaming Mahima.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel when Usha reminded her?
qa.a: Embarrassed that she had forgotten, then grateful that Usha was kind about it, so she returned them with a toffee.

grounding: A girl lends her friend her sketch pens freely and later asks for them back politely.

passage: Omkar here. I want to remember what happened with my watercolour box this term. The first time Seema forgot her colours, I pushed my box across without thinking. It felt nice to see her face relax. The second time, I did it again. By the fifth time, my red cake was nearly gone and my best brush had gone home with her twice. I felt a small, sour knot in my stomach, and I didn't like feeling that about a friend. So on Friday I said, 'Seema, you can always share my colours in class. But please bring yours too, and give my brush back today.' She blinked, then nodded and dug it out of her bag. We still share. I just don't feel sour any more.

qa.q: Which colour cake was nearly gone?
qa.a: The red cake.

qa.q: What did the sour knot in Omkar's stomach mean?
qa.a: Omkar was starting to feel used and a little resentful after lending again and again, and didn't like feeling that way about a friend.

qa.q: What boundary did Omkar set, and why did it help?
qa.a: Omkar kept sharing in class but asked Seema to bring her own colours and return the brush, so the kindness stopped turning sour.

qa.q: How might Seema have felt when Omkar spoke up?
qa.a: Surprised at first, since she blinked, then willing; she nodded and gave the brush back.

grounding: A child keeps lending colours to a friend but sets a polite limit when the lending starts to feel one-sided.

passage: Exam week, and Binita had one evening to revise three chapters. At four o'clock the phone rang. 'Binu, my bestie!' Sangeeta sang. 'Can you send photos of your history notes? All of them?' Binita stared at the wall. Sangeeta hadn't sat with her at lunch once this month. She only ever called like this, sweet as jaggery, when she needed something. Binita's chest felt heavy. 'No, I can't tonight,' she said. 'Oh, why? It's just five minutes of your time.' 'No. Good luck with revision.' She hung up, hands shaking a little. Then she thought of Lata, who had saved her a seat on the bus every day without being asked, and sent her a message: 'Study together tomorrow?'

qa.q: How many chapters did Binita have to revise?
qa.a: Three chapters.

qa.q: Why did Binita's chest feel heavy?
qa.a: She felt used, because Sangeeta was only sweet when she needed something and ignored her the rest of the time.

qa.q: What did Binita do that a wise friend would?
qa.a: She said no without long explanations and reached out to Lata, who is kind to her without any reason.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta see Binita's refusal?
qa.a: She may be surprised and annoyed, since she expected Binita to hand over her notes as usual.

grounding: During exam week a girl refuses a classmate who is only nice when she needs something, and turns to a genuinely kind friend.

passage: In the colony park in Pune, Simran came skipping over, all smiles. 'Ankita, your new cycle is so pretty. Can I take it to the market and back?' Ankita remembered last Sunday, struggling up the stairs with two heavy grocery bags while Simran walked right past, busy with her phone. And the Diwali party, where Simran hadn't said one word to her. It was always like this: honey when she wanted something, nothing otherwise. Ankita felt a flash of hurt. 'No, not today,' she said. Simran pouted. 'Why not?' 'Just no.' Simran flounced off. Moin from the third floor, who had helped Ankita pick up spilled tomatoes that Sunday, wandered over with a football. 'Want to play?' Ankita grinned. 'Yes.'

qa.q: What did Simran ask to take to the market?
qa.a: Ankita's new cycle.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she remembered last Sunday?
qa.a: A flash of hurt; she felt used, because Simran is only sweet when she wants something.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying a short no without explaining, and turning to Moin, who helped her without being asked.

qa.q: What would change if Simran had been kind to Ankita all along?
qa.a: Ankita might have been happy to lend the cycle, because there would already be trust between them.

grounding: A girl says no to a neighbour who is only friendly when she wants something, and notices who is kind without a reason.

passage: The canteen at Tanvir's new school was louder than a railway station. He carried his tiffin past table after table where everyone already had a place. He sat at the very end of one bench and ate his parathas slowly, pretending to read the menu board. His throat felt tight. Nobody looked up. After lunch, a group ran out to play kho-kho. Tanvir's feet wanted to go back to class. Instead he walked to the edge of the ground and smiled at a girl tying her laces. 'Can I play?' Deepika shrugged. 'We need one more on our side anyway.' He was caught in the first minute. But on the way back, Deepika said, 'You run fast. Sit with us tomorrow?'

qa.q: What game did the group play after lunch?
qa.a: Kho-kho.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel eating at the end of the bench?
qa.a: Lonely and nervous; his throat felt tight, and he pretended to read the menu so nobody would notice.

qa.q: What small step helped Tanvir?
qa.a: Smiling at someone and asking to join the game, instead of going back to class alone.

qa.q: How might Deepika see the new boy?
qa.a: As a newcomer who runs fast; she is easygoing about it and invites him to sit with them.

grounding: A new boy eats lunch alone on his first day, then takes a small step and asks to join a game.

passage:
Monday. Lalit's first day at the new school in Bhopal. At lunch he sat under the neem tree with his dabba and watched the others laugh in groups. Nobody came over. At home he told Papa, 'It's the worst.' Papa said, 'First days usually are.'
Thursday. Lalit tried one thing. He sat on the bench beside Aditi, who was reading a comic, and asked, 'Is that the one with the flying cow?' She laughed and showed him. They didn't talk much after that, but it was something.
Three weeks later. Aditi saved him a seat, and two boys from the back row asked Lalit to join their cricket at break. He still missed his old gang, but lunch no longer felt like the longest part of the day.

qa.q: Where did Lalit sit at lunch on his first day?
qa.a: Under the neem tree with his dabba.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling on Monday evening when he spoke to Papa?
qa.a: Lonely and discouraged; he called the day the worst.

qa.q: What step did Lalit try on Thursday?
qa.a: Sitting beside Aditi and asking about her comic, a small way to start talking.

qa.q: How might Aditi see Lalit's question about the comic?
qa.a: As a friendly opening; she laughed and showed him, and weeks later she saved him a seat.

grounding: Over three weeks a lonely new boy takes small steps at lunch and slowly makes friends.

passage:
'Rehana! Can you see me? The screen's frozen.'
'Now I can. Arohi, you cut your hair!'
'Mumbai is so humid. It kept sticking to my neck.' Arohi laughed, then her voice went thin. 'I miss our terrace. I miss the chaat uncle. I miss you so much, it's silly.'
'It's not silly. We all went quiet at practice when Coach read out your name.'
'Really?'
'Really. Did you make any friends there?'
Arohi picked at the blanket. 'A girl called Nisha asked me to join the dance club. I said no. It felt like cheating on you all.'
'Cheating? Arohi, go! Then you can teach me the steps on Sunday's call.'
Arohi was quiet. 'Okay. Sunday call, same time?'
'Same time. Every Sunday.'

qa.q: Which club did Nisha invite Arohi to join?
qa.a: The dance club.

qa.q: Why did Arohi say no to the dance club?
qa.a: She missed her old friends so much that joining felt like cheating on them; she felt sad and a little guilty.

qa.q: What helps Arohi keep old friends and make room for new ones?
qa.a: Weekly Sunday calls with Rehana, and saying yes to the dance club so she can share the steps.

qa.q: How does Rehana see Arohi making new friends?
qa.a: As a good thing, not a betrayal; she urges Arohi to go and share it with her 🤍

grounding: A girl who has moved city tells her old friend how much she misses her, and is encouraged to stay in touch and make new friends too.

passage: When we moved from Lucknow to Hyderabad last year, I refused to unpack my boxes for a month. My name is Nazia, and I was sure that if I kept them taped, we might somehow go back. I missed the azaan from our old mosque, the kebab smoke in the lane, and most of all Yusuf, who lived two doors down and taught me to fly kites. I wrote him long letters with pressed flowers inside. Then one letter from him said he had joined a kite club and made a friend called Ravi. My stomach dropped, and then something loosened. If Yusuf could keep me and still make room for Ravi, maybe I could do the same. That evening, I unpacked my first box.

qa.q: Who taught Nazia to fly kites?
qa.a: Yusuf, who lived two doors down.

qa.q: Why did Nazia keep the boxes taped?
qa.a: Nazia felt so homesick for Lucknow that unpacking felt like giving up hope of going back.

qa.q: What helped Nazia stop living only in the past?
qa.a: Seeing Yusuf keep their friendship while making a new friend, which showed there was room for both; then Nazia unpacked the first box.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel reading Nazia's long letters?
qa.a: Missed and cared for, since they came with pressed flowers; they show the friendship still matters.

grounding: A child who moved city misses an old friend deeply, writes to him, and slowly makes room for a new life.

passage: The new school's office smelled of floor polish and old files. Nandini sat on a plastic chair while the clerk, Jaya Aunty, stamped her transfer certificate. Papa smiled at the notice board. 'Look, they have a swimming team!' Nandini's jaw tightened. 'I hate this place. I hate this whole city. Nobody asked me.' The clerk kept stamping, eyes down. Papa's smile faded. He sat beside her. 'You're right. Nobody asked you. Tell me what you miss.' 'My bench by the window. Pooja. The bakery near the old school. Everything.' Her voice cracked. Papa didn't promise anything or tell her she would love it here. He just listened, nodding, until the clerk called her name.

qa.q: What did the new school's office smell of?
qa.a: Floor polish and old files.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling behind her tight jaw and 'I hate this place'?
qa.a: She was angry and resentful that the move was decided without her, and sad about everything she had left.

qa.q: Which choice by Papa helped, and why?
qa.a: He agreed nobody had asked her and invited her to say what she missed, then listened without trying to fix it.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when Nandini says she hates the city?
qa.a: Hurt and a little guilty, since his smile faded, but he chose to sit beside her and listen.

grounding: In a new school's office a girl says she hates the move, and her father listens to what she misses without fixing it.

passage:
The night before the move, Disha refused to help pack and slammed her door so hard the photo frames rattled. 'You never even asked me!'
Friday, the first week in Guwahati. At dinner, Jatin chattered about his new class. Disha pushed her plate away. 'I hate it here. I hate you both for this.' Mummy's eyes filled, but she stayed at the table. 'That's a big feeling. What do you miss most?' Disha listed it, crying: her swimming coach, her friend's terrace, the lane with the gulmohar tree.
Sunday. Mummy and Papa didn't argue or promise it would get better. They asked if she wanted to call her coach. She did. Afterwards Disha sat on the new balcony, still angry, but lighter.

qa.q: What did Disha do the night before the move?
qa.a: She refused to help pack and slammed her door.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling at Friday's dinner?
qa.a: Angry and resentful at her parents for moving without asking, and sad about everything she had lost.

qa.q: What did the parents do that helped?
qa.a: They stayed, asked what she missed and listened without arguing or promising; on Sunday they offered a call to her coach.

qa.q: What was it like for Mummy when Disha said she hated them?
qa.a: Painful; her eyes filled, but she stayed at the table and asked a gentle question.

grounding: Over several days a girl voices anger at her parents for a move, and they listen and help her name what she misses.

passage: On Kunal's first morning at the school in Salt Lake, Kolkata, the class teacher, Mrs Bose, led him down a corridor that seemed to go on forever. 'Deepak will be your buddy this week,' she said. A boy with a gap in his teeth waved. Kunal's shoulders loosened a little. At break, Deepak showed him the water cooler, the shortcut to the library, and which staircase the seniors ruled. 'Can I ask something silly?' Kunal said. 'When do we get PT?' 'Not silly. Thursdays. Bring white shoes, or Sir makes you run extra.' Kunal wrote it in his diary. By the last bell he had asked eleven questions, and Deepak had answered every one without laughing.

qa.q: Which day is PT?
qa.a: Thursdays.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel when Deepak waved?
qa.a: A little safer and less nervous; his shoulders loosened.

qa.q: What helped Kunal learn the school's ways quickly?
qa.a: Accepting Deepak's help and asking questions, even ones he thought were silly, and writing the answers down.

qa.q: How might Deepak see his job as a buddy?
qa.a: As something to take seriously; he answered every question without laughing, which made Kunal feel welcome 😊

grounding: A new boy trusts the buddy his teacher assigns, asks many questions and learns the school's ways.

passage:
'Afreen, you'll work with Sangeeta in the lab today,' Ma'am said. 'She knows where everything is.'
Sangeeta pulled out a stool. 'Hi. Goggles first, or Ma'am gets cross.'
'Where do I put my bag?' Afreen whispered.
'On the hook under the bench. Here.'
A boy at the next table smirked. 'New girl doesn't even know the hooks.'
Sangeeta didn't look up. 'She's been here two days. You didn't know the hooks for a month.'
Afreen laughed despite herself. 'Can I ask how you're mixing that? At my old school we did it differently.'
'Show me your way. Then I'll show you ours.'
By the end of the period, their test tube had turned the right shade of blue. Afreen wrote the reading neatly, her hands steady now.

qa.q: Where did Sangeeta tell Afreen to put her bag?
qa.a: On the hook under the bench.

qa.q: How can you tell Afreen's nervousness eased during the lesson?
qa.a: She laughed at Sangeeta's reply and her hands were steady by the end; she felt safer and more trusting.

qa.q: What made the pairing work?
qa.a: Afreen asked questions and shared her old school's way, and Sangeeta explained without treating her as lesser.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta see Afreen being new?
qa.a: As no reason to look down on her; she defends Afreen and wants to learn her way too.

grounding: A new girl accepts help from a lab partner her teacher assigns, asks questions and is treated as an equal.

passage: Pankaj's family had moved from Gaya to a village near Ludhiana for his father's work at the rice mill. In his first week, whenever he answered in class, three boys at the back repeated his words in a sing-song voice, and everyone giggled. His ears burned. At night he practised talking like them in front of the mirror, then stopped. That was his Dadi's way of speaking too. On Friday it happened again at the handpump. This time Pankaj went straight to Masterji. Masterji listened, called the three boys over that same afternoon, told them the mocking stops now, and moved Pankaj's seat to the front. Mehak, from the front row, said, 'Say "sattu" again. I like how you say it.' He did, and she smiled.

qa.q: Where did the boys mock Pankaj on Friday?
qa.a: At the handpump.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj practise talking like the others, then stop?
qa.a: He felt ashamed of his accent, then remembered it was his Dadi's way of speaking too and felt proud of it again.

qa.q: What worked once the teasing continued?
qa.a: Telling Masterji, who spoke to the boys that same afternoon, and noticing kinder classmates like Mehak.

qa.q: How might Mehak see Pankaj's way of speaking?
qa.a: As something she likes, not something to laugh at.

grounding: A boy whose accent is mocked in a new village school keeps his way of speaking, tells a teacher, and finds a kinder classmate.

passage: Priscila had moved from Recife to a small town in Scotland in January. In her first week, when she said 'thank you' with rolled r's in the dinner hall, two girls copied her in a squeaky voice, and the whole table laughed. Priscila's cheeks went hot, and she decided to stay silent. On Wednesday they did it again during PE. After class Priscila walked to Mr Reid, her legs shaky. 'They keep copying how I talk.' Mr Reid thanked her for telling him, spoke with the two girls before lunch, and said he would keep an eye on the dinner hall. Freya, who sat next to her in maths, asked, 'How do you say "friend" in Portuguese?' 'Amiga.' Freya grinned. 'Amiga. Did I say it right?'

qa.q: Where did Priscila move from?
qa.a: From Recife.

qa.q: Why did Priscila decide to stay silent after the dinner hall?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and hurt when the girls copied her voice and the whole table laughed.

qa.q: What did Priscila do when the mocking continued, and what happened next?
qa.a: She told Mr Reid, who spoke with the girls before lunch that day and promised to keep an eye on the dinner hall.

qa.q: How does Freya see Priscila's language?
qa.a: With curiosity and respect; she wants to learn the Portuguese word for friend.

grounding: A girl whose accent is mocked at a new school abroad tells a teacher when it continues and finds a kinder classmate.

passage: On Monday a new boy stood at the front of Clara's classroom in Melbourne, holding his bag strap with both hands. 'This is Bao,' said Ms Hart. 'He's just moved from Da Nang.' Clara stared at his dinosaur pencil case. She wanted to ask about it, but her face went warm and she looked down at her desk. At recess Bao stood by the fence, alone, kicking at wood chips. Clara counted to ten in her head, then walked over. 'Hi. I like your pencil case. Do you want to see where the handball court is?' Bao's face lit up. 'Yes, please.' She showed him the court, the drinking taps and the shady spot behind the library. By lunch, he was teaching her a clapping game.

qa.q: Where did Bao move from?
qa.a: Da Nang.

qa.q: What was Clara feeling when she first wanted to ask about the pencil case?
qa.a: Curious but shy; her face went warm and she looked down at her desk.

qa.q: What small step changed Bao's first day?
qa.a: Clara walked over at recess, said she liked his pencil case and showed him around.

qa.q: What was it like for Bao standing alone by the fence?
qa.a: Probably lonely and unsure, which is why his face lit up when Clara invited him.

grounding: A shy, curious girl greets a new boy, shows him around and invites him to play.

passage: A new boy arrived at the sports hostel in the middle of term, carrying a steel trunk almost as big as himself. 'Lokesh, from Nagpur,' the warden announced at dinner. 'He joins the athletics squad tomorrow.' Trisha, who had lived at the hostel for two years, watched him sit at the end of the table and stare at his dal. She wanted to know if he was a sprinter or a jumper, but the question stuck in her throat. Next morning at practice, he stood alone at the edge of the track. Trisha jogged over, heart thumping. 'I'm Trisha. Long jump. Want me to show you the warm-up?' Lokesh nodded fast. At breakfast she waved him over to their table, and he came.

qa.q: What did Lokesh carry when he arrived?
qa.a: A steel trunk almost as big as himself.

qa.q: Why did the question stick in Trisha's throat?
qa.a: She was curious about him but shy, and her heart was still thumping when she finally went over.

qa.q: How did Trisha help Lokesh's first days?
qa.a: She introduced herself, offered to show him the warm-up and waved him to her table at breakfast.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel sitting alone and staring at his dal?
qa.a: Lonely and nervous in a new place mid-term, so Trisha's invitation probably felt like a relief.

grounding: At a sports hostel a curious but shy girl welcomes a new boy and includes him.

passage: At her new school in Chandigarh, Bhavna had decided to be cool. So she'd said she didn't care about studies, that cartoons were babyish, and that she had once flown on a plane. Then the class trip to the planetarium got stuck in a flooded underpass for three hours. Rain drummed on the bus roof. Baljeet, beside her, was reading a book about planets. 'You'd find this boring,' he said. Bhavna's jaw ached from shrugging and pretending. She loved planets. She had a glow-in-the-dark star map at home. By the second hour, she was too tired to keep it up. 'Actually, I know all of Saturn's big moons,' she said. Baljeet stared, then grinned and moved the book between them.

qa.q: Where did the bus get stuck?
qa.a: In a flooded underpass.

qa.q: What does Bhavna's aching jaw suggest?
qa.a: She was exhausted and uncomfortable from pretending to be someone she wasn't.

qa.q: What could Bhavna keep from her fresh start, and what could she drop?
qa.a: She can keep making new friends in a new place but drop the fake act, since being honest about planets made Baljeet share his book.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see Bhavna after she mentions Saturn's moons?
qa.a: Surprised and pleased to find a fellow planet fan, so he shares his book with her.

grounding: Stuck on a long bus ride, a girl trying to seem cool at a new school grows tired of pretending and shows her real interest.

passage: At his old school in Mysuru, everyone had called Wasim 'Encyclopedia'. At the new one in Bengaluru, he wanted to be someone else. So when Tejas and the others joked about hating maths, Wasim laughed too and hid his test under his bag. He joined the drama club, which he'd never dared before, and loved it. But hiding everything else was tiring. Every evening his cheeks hurt from fake laughing. Then, at rehearsal, Tejas forgot his lines and sighed, 'I wish I were clever like you. You topped the maths test, didn't you? Sir told us.' Wasim froze. 'You knew?' 'Everyone knew. Why do you hide it?' Wasim had no answer. The next day he brought his test out and helped Tejas with fractions.

qa.q: What had everyone called Wasim at his old school?
qa.a: Encyclopedia.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel about hiding his marks every day?
qa.a: Worn out and tired; his cheeks hurt from fake laughing.

qa.q: Which part of Wasim's fresh start was worth keeping?
qa.a: Joining the drama club, something new he enjoyed; hiding his cleverness was the part to drop.

qa.q: How does Tejas see Wasim's cleverness?
qa.a: As something to admire, not mock; he even wishes he were clever like Wasim.

grounding: A boy at a new school tries a new hobby but tires of hiding who he is, and chooses to be himself.

passage: Every Sunday, Jaya borrowed her mother's phone at the tea stall by the village bus stand and sent Pema a long voice note about the new school in Palampur, the apple orchard and the goat that chewed her dupatta. At first Pema sent long ones back from Gangtok. Then short ones. Then just a heart. This week, nothing. Jaya sat on the stone wall, feeling hollow. Had Pema forgotten her? Her mother sat down beside her. 'Pema has a new class too, new homework, new friends. It's no one's fault.' Jaya thought about that. Then she recorded a short, cheerful note: 'Miss you. Summer holidays, I'm coming to Gangtok. Save me a momo.' She meant it, and it didn't hurt quite so much.

qa.q: Where did Jaya send her voice notes from?
qa.a: The tea stall by the village bus stand.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel on the stone wall this week?
qa.a: Hollow and hurt, worried that Pema had forgotten her.

qa.q: What wise step did Jaya take after talking with her mother?
qa.a: She sent a short, cheerful note and planned a visit in the summer holidays, instead of blaming Pema.

qa.q: How might Pema's life explain the shorter replies?
qa.a: Pema has a new class, homework and friends too, so replying less may not mean she cares less.

grounding: A girl who moved away notices her old friend replying less, accepts it is no one's fault, and plans a holiday visit.

passage: Esther had moved from Lagos to Manchester eighteen months ago. On her tenth birthday, she kept checking her mum's tablet all evening. Chidi, her best friend since nursery, didn't call. The next day a message came: 'Sorry!! Happy birthday! Football finals yesterday.' Esther read it three times. It stung. Over the Christmas holidays they finally video-called. Chidi talked about boys she didn't know, and Esther talked about snow he'd never seen. There were long pauses. Afterwards Esther lay on her bed, sad but not angry. 'We're just far,' she told Mum. 'Nobody did anything wrong.' Then she opened her drawer and looked at the bead bracelet Chidi had given her. She still wore it on Sundays.

qa.q: What did Chidi's message say he had been busy with?
qa.a: Football finals.

qa.q: How did Esther feel after the Christmas call?
qa.a: Sad but not angry; she had accepted that distance was changing things.

qa.q: What healthy way did Esther find to hold on to the friendship?
qa.a: Accepting the drift without blaming Chidi, staying in touch in the holidays and still wearing his bead bracelet on Sundays 🤍

qa.q: How might Chidi feel after missing Esther's birthday?
qa.a: Guilty and sorry, as his double exclamation marks suggest, even though his life in Lagos has become busy.

grounding: A girl who moved abroad feels her old friendship fading, accepts it is nobody's fault, and stays fond of her friend.
